prompt: Inside a computer, information is represented by currents, voltage differences, or, for permanent storage:
explanation: Currents and voltage differences while the machine runs, orientation of magnetic material when it has to survive a power cut.

why.a: Correct. Magnetic orientation is the deck's example of permanent storage.
why.b: Wrong. Temperature is never used to carry information here.
why.c: Wrong. Resistance is not one of the three the slide names.
why.d: Wrong. The clock paces the machine; it does not store its data.

prompt: Why are numbers usually represented within a computer in base 2?

options.text: Because a single circuit or piece of magnetic material is often regarded as being in one of two states
Because base 2 arithmetic is more accurate than base 10
Because base 2 takes up less space on the page
Because programmers find binary easier to read

explanation: Two physical states, so one binary digit. The representation follows the hardware, not the other way round.

why.a: Correct. Two states means it can represent a binary digit, and base 2 follows from that.
why.b: Wrong. Accuracy is a matter of how many bits you use, not which base the hardware works in.
why.c: Wrong, and reversed: taking up less space on the page is the deck's reason for displaying in hexadecimal.
why.d: Wrong. The deck says the opposite: hexadecimal is used for display because it is easier to remember.

prompt: A single electronic circuit or piece of magnetic material is often regarded as being in one of two states, so it can be used to represent a binary digit.
explanation: This is the sentence that connects the physics to the arithmetic, and everything else in the deck rests on it.

why.true: Correct. Two states, one binary digit, therefore base 2.
why.false: Wrong. The slide states this directly as the reason numbers are represented in base 2.

prompt: In the digit sequence formula, what is the last term, the one for the rightmost digit?

options.text: a nought times base to the power 0
a nought times base to the power 1
a nought only, with no base at all

explanation: The rightmost digit is multiplied by base to the power 0, which is 1. That is why it contributes its own face value.

why.a: Correct. The exponent counts up from 0 at the right.
why.b: Wrong. Power 1 belongs to the digit one place to the left.
why.c: Wrong. Multiplying by the base itself is the same mistake as power 1.
why.d: Wrong in form, even though the value works out the same, because the formula is written with the base to the power 0.

prompt: In a digit sequence of n digits, the leftmost digit is multiplied by base to the power {{1}}.
explanation: n minus 1. With n digits the exponents run from n minus 1 down to 0, which is n values in all.

topic: why hexadecimal is used for display
prompt: Although data is stored in binary, it is often displayed in hexadecimal because:

options.text: It takes up less space on the page and is easier to remember

explanation: Less space, easier to remember. Hexadecimal is a convenience for people; the machine is still in binary.

why.a: Correct. Both reasons are on the slide.
why.b: Wrong. The hardware has two states, so it works in base 2.
why.c: Wrong. The arithmetic is the same numbers either way; only the notation changes.
why.d: Wrong. Binary represents any number hexadecimal can, just with four times as many digits.

topic: why hexadecimal is used for display
prompt: Hexadecimal is base {{1}}.
explanation: Base 16, which is 2 to the power 4, and that is exactly why four bits map onto one hex digit.

prompt: To convert an integer into a digit string in a base, you repeatedly divide by the base. The digits are:

options.text: The remainders, generated from right to left
The remainders, generated from left to right
The quotients, generated from right to left
The quotients, generated from left to right

explanation: Remainders, right to left. The first remainder you get is the last digit you write, which is why the answer is read bottom to top.

why.a: Correct. Remainders, and they are generated from right to left.
why.b: Wrong direction. Writing them left to right reverses the number.
why.c: Wrong. The quotients are what you keep dividing; they are not the digits.
why.d: Wrong on both counts.

prompt: To convert an integer into a digit string in a base, repeatedly {{1}} the number by the base.
explanation: Divide. Going the other way, from a base into decimal, you multiply instead.

prompt: In the toBase program, what happens when n is negative?

options.text: It returns a minus sign followed by toBase of the positive value
It takes the two's complement first

explanation: The program handles the sign separately, prefixing a minus and recursing on the positive value. Returning 0 is the case for n equal to zero.

why.a: Correct. It returns minus, joined to toBase of minus n.
why.b: Wrong. That is the branch for n equal to 0.
why.c: Wrong. Throwing an Invalid digit error belongs to fromDigit, in the other program.
why.d: Wrong. The two's complement is a hardware representation, and this program produces a printable digit string.

prompt: In the toDigit routine, what is returned when n is 10 or more?

options.text: n plus the character a, minus 10

explanation: Digits 0 to 9 come from adding the character 0. Values from 10 upward become letters, by adding the character a and subtracting 10 so that 10 lands on a.

why.a: Correct. That maps 10 to a, 11 to b, and so on.
why.b: Wrong. That is the branch for n less than 10.
why.c: Wrong. Subtracting 10 alone gives a number, not a character.
why.d: Wrong. Nothing in the routine repeats a character.

prompt: Converting decimal 13 to binary by repeated division gives:
explanation: 13 over 2 is 6 remainder 1, 6 over 2 is 3 remainder 0, 3 over 2 is 1 remainder 1, 1 over 2 is 0 remainder 1. Read bottom to top: 1101.

why.a: Correct. 8 plus 4 plus 1 is 13.
why.b: Wrong. 1011 is 11, and it is what you get by reading the remainders in the order they came out.
why.c: Wrong. 1110 is 14.
why.d: Wrong. 0111 is 7.

prompt: Dividing 13 by 2 gives quotient 6 remainder {{1}}, and dividing 6 by 2 gives quotient 3 remainder {{2}}.
explanation: Remainder 1 then remainder 0. The remainders in order are 1, 0, 1, 1, and reading them bottom to top gives 1101.

prompt: Converting from a digit string in a base to an integer is described as being like:
explanation: Like evaluating a polynomial: process the digits left to right, multiply what you have so far by the base, add the next digit.

why.a: Correct, and the method is Horner's scheme in all but name.
why.b: Wrong. Nothing is being solved for.
why.c: Wrong. Complements belong to signed number representation.
why.d: Wrong. Shifting left multiplies by 2, which is a different operation covered two slides later.

prompt: Process the digits from left to right, multiply what you have so far by the base, and {{1}} the next digit.
explanation: Add. Multiply then add, once per digit, is the whole method.

prompt: The fromDigit routine accepts letters a to z as digits. What is the highest base it therefore allows?
explanation: Ten digits plus twenty six letters is thirty six symbols, and the deck's comment says so: allow up to base 36.

why.a: Correct, and the slide comments it in the code.
why.b: Wrong. That counts only the letters and forgets the ten digits.
why.c: Wrong. Base 16 uses only a to f.
why.d: Wrong. That is the digits alone, with no letters.

prompt: In the fromBase routine, what does the accumulation step do on each character?

options.text: result equals result times base, plus fromDigit of the character
result equals result plus base, times fromDigit of the character
result equals result divided by base, plus the character
result equals fromDigit of the character only

explanation: Multiply the running total by the base, then add the new digit. It is the polynomial evaluation from the previous slide written as code.

why.a: Correct, and it matches the worked example: 0 times 2 plus 1, then 1 times 2 plus 1, and so on.
why.b: Wrong. The operations are the wrong way round.
why.c: Wrong. Dividing belongs to the other direction, decimal into a base.
why.d: Wrong. That would discard every digit but the last.

prompt: Evaluating binary 1101 left to right gives 1, then 3, then 6, then:
explanation: 6 times 2 plus 1 is 13. The four steps are 0 times 2 plus 1 is 1, 1 times 2 plus 1 is 3, 3 times 2 plus 0 is 6, 6 times 2 plus 1 is 13.

why.a: Correct, and it agrees with the other direction, where 13 converted to binary gave 1101.
why.b: Wrong. 12 would need a final digit of 0.
why.c: Wrong. 11 is 1011, a different bit pattern.
why.d: Wrong. 14 is 1110.

prompt: The third step of evaluating 1101 is {{1}} times 2 plus 0, which is {{2}}.
explanation: 3 times 2 plus 0 is 6. The running total doubles at every step and picks up the next bit.

prompt: The arithmetic in a base conversion computation can be performed in any base you like.
explanation: The deck says so. The method does not care what base you do the sums in; only the answer's notation changes.

why.true: Correct. The slide closes with exactly this remark.
why.false: Wrong. The deck states it plainly after the worked example.

prompt: Conversion between binary and hexadecimal amounts to grouping or ungrouping bits into sets of:
explanation: Four, because 16 is 2 to the power 4. Sets of three would give octal, and sets of eight give a byte.

why.a: Correct. One hex digit is exactly four bits.
why.b: Wrong. Three bits is one octal digit.
why.c: Wrong. Eight bits is a byte, which is two hex digits.
why.d: Wrong. Two bits would give base 4, which this course does not use.

prompt: Using the conversion table, hexadecimal 3fc is {{1}} in binary.
explanation: 3 is 0011, f is 1111, c is 1100. This is the number the deck then halves two slides later to get 1fe.

prompt: The deck groups 110101101011101 as 110, 1011, 0101, 1101 and prints the answer 6B5C. Working it yourself, what is the correct hexadecimal?
explanation: The last group is 1101, which is 13 decimal, and 13 in hexadecimal is D. The slide's own working line reads 13D=CH, which is where the slip enters, and the printed answer 6B5C carries it through. Everything else on the slide is right: 110 is 6, 1011 is B, 0101 is 5.

why.a: Correct. 6, B, 5, D. Take the slide's grouping but finish the last digit yourself.
why.b: Wrong, and this is the answer as printed. 13 decimal is D, not C, so the final digit is wrong on the slide.
why.c: Wrong. B is 11, so 6B5B would need a final group of 1011.
why.d: Wrong. The second group 1011 is B, not C.

prompt: The binary group 1101 converts to the hexadecimal digit C.
explanation: 1101 is 13 decimal, and 13 is hexadecimal D. C is 12, which is 1100. The deck's conversion slide prints this the wrong way round, so trust the arithmetic rather than the slide.

why.true: Wrong, and it repeats the slide's slip. C is 12, whose bit pattern is 1100.

prompt: What is hexadecimal A34E in decimal?
explanation: 10 times 4096 is 40960, plus 3 times 256 is 768, plus 4 times 16 is 64, plus 14. That is 40960 plus 768 plus 64 plus 14, giving 41806.

why.a: Correct. 41806. 10 times 4096 is 40960, plus 3 times 256 is 768, plus 4 times 16 is 64, plus 14.
why.b: Wrong. That takes E as 10 rather than 14.
why.c: Wrong. That is the A term alone, with the other three digits dropped.
why.d: Wrong by a factor of ten, a digit lost in transcription.

prompt: Expanding A34E, the digit A is worth {{1}} in decimal and the digit E is worth {{2}}.
explanation: A is 10 and E is 14. Counting up from A gives A 10, B 11, C 12, D 13, E 14, F 15.

prompt: What is hexadecimal A34E in binary?
explanation: A is 1010, 3 is 0011, 4 is 0100, E is 1110. Four digits, four groups of four bits.

why.a: Correct. A is 1010, 3 is 0011, 4 is 0100, E is 1110.
why.b: Wrong. The last group is E, which is 1110, not 1010.
why.c: Wrong. The first group is A, which is 1010, not 1011.
why.d: Wrong. The middle two digits are 3 then 4, so 0011 then 0100.

prompt: In A34E, the hexadecimal digit E is {{1}} in binary.
explanation: 1110, which is 14. 1111 would be F and 1101 would be D.

prompt: To divide a binary number by 2, you:

options.text: Shift the digits right by one place
Shift the digits left by one place

explanation: Right shift halves, left shift doubles. In base 2 the shift is the arithmetic.

why.a: Correct. Every bit moves one place towards the low end, so each is worth half what it was.
why.b: Wrong. Shifting left multiplies by 2.
why.c: Wrong. The one's complement negates; it does not divide.
why.d: Wrong. That gives zero.

prompt: Shifting the digits of a binary number left by one place multiplies it by 2.
explanation: It does, and the deck gives it as the companion to the right shift. It is the same reason that adding a zero to the end of a decimal number multiplies it by ten.

why.true: Correct. Left is multiply, right is divide.
why.false: Wrong. The deck says we can multiply or divide a binary number by 2 by shifting left or right.

prompt: Computing 3fc divided by 2 in hexadecimal gives:
explanation: Decode 3fc as 0011 1111 1100, shift the bits right by 1 to get 0001 1111 1110, and encode again to get 1fe.

why.a: Correct. 1fe, and you can check it: 1fe is 510, and 3fc is 1020.
why.b: Wrong. The last group after the shift is 1110, which is e, not 6.
why.c: Wrong, and that is 3fc shifted the other way, so it is 3fc times 2.
why.d: Wrong. The leading digit must halve too.

prompt: To halve a hexadecimal number, decode it into binary, perform the {{1}}, then {{2}} the digits again.
explanation: Decode, shift, encode. Hexadecimal has no shift of its own, so you borrow binary's.

prompt: Binary Coded Decimal is:

options.text: A type of binary code used to represent a given decimal number in an equivalent binary form
The pure binary value of a decimal number
A method of representing negative numbers
A character code for letters and symbols

explanation: BCD codes a decimal number digit by digit, which is why 59 becomes 0101 1001 rather than the pure binary 111011.

why.a: Correct. It is the deck's definition word for word.
why.b: Wrong, and that is the distinction that matters: pure binary converts the whole number, BCD codes each digit separately.
why.c: Wrong. Negative numbers use sign magnitude, one's complement or two's complement.
why.d: Wrong. Character codes are ASCII, EBCDIC and Unicode.

prompt: BCD stands for Binary {{1}} Decimal.
explanation: Coded. Test 1 asked for this expansion directly, with Binary Control Digit and Binary Character Decimal among the distractors.

prompt: The main advantage of BCD is that it allows:

options.text: Easy conversion to decimal digits for printing or display, and faster calculations
More numbers to be stored in the same number of bits
Negative numbers to be represented without a sign bit
Letters and digits to share one encoding

explanation: Easy conversion for printing or display, and faster calculations. BCD trades density for convenience, which is why it suits displays.

why.a: Correct, both halves are on the slide.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the opposite: BCD wastes six of the sixteen patterns in every four bits.
why.c: Wrong. BCD says nothing about sign.
why.d: Wrong. That would be an alphanumeric code.

prompt: BCD is chosen because it stores decimal numbers in fewer bits than pure binary does.
explanation: The advantage claimed is easy conversion for printing or display and faster calculations, not compactness. Coding each digit in four bits uses more space, not less.

why.true: Wrong. BCD is less compact than pure binary, since six of every sixteen four-bit patterns go unused.
why.false: Correct. The stated advantages are conversion for display and faster calculations.

prompt: Select the three types of BCD the deck names.
explanation: 8421, 5421 and 4221. Excess-3 is a code in this deck too, but it is non-weighted and is taught separately from BCD.

why.a: Correct, 8421 is the familiar one.
why.b: Correct, 5421 is second.
why.c: Correct, 4221 is third.
why.d: Wrong. 2421 is a real BCD variant in the wider literature, but it is not one of the three this deck names.
why.e: Wrong. Excess-3 is a non-weighted code, and the deck introduces it as a separate topic.

prompt: The deck names {{1}} different types of BCD.
In the names 8421, 5421 and 4221, what do the four numbers represent?

options.text: The weights of the relevant bits
The decimal digits the code can represent
The order in which the bits are transmitted
The number of bits in each group

explanation: Weights. Each of the four bit positions carries the weight its name gives, and the digit is the sum of the weights whose bit is 1.

why.a: Correct, and that is what makes BCD a weighted code.
why.b: Wrong. Every one of the three codes represents the digits 0 to 9.
why.c: Wrong. Transmission order is not discussed anywhere in this deck.
why.d: Wrong. All three use four bits per digit, which is why all four names have four numbers.

prompt: The weights of 8421 BCD are 8, 4, {{1}} and {{2}}.
explanation: 8, 4, 2, 1, which are the ordinary powers of two, and that is why 8421 BCD looks like plain binary for a single digit.

topic: why BCD is a weighted code
prompt: BCD is a weighted code, meaning that:

options.text: The sum of the weights of the binary digits whose value is 1 equals the decimal digit they represent
Some digits are more important than others and are stored first
The code adds a fixed amount to each decimal digit

explanation: Add up the weights where the bit is 1. That single rule decodes 8421, 5421 and 4221 alike.

why.a: Correct. It is the definition of a weighted code.
why.b: Wrong. Weight here is a numeric value, not a priority.
why.c: Wrong, and that is Excess-3, which adds 3 to each digit and is explicitly non-weighted.
why.d: Wrong. Self-complementing is a property of Excess-3.

topic: why BCD is a weighted code
prompt: In 4221 BCD the bit pattern 1111 has weights that sum to {{1}}, which is the decimal digit it represents.
explanation: 4 plus 2 plus 2 plus 1 is 9, which is why the deck gives 1111 as the 4221 code for 9. In 8421 the same pattern would sum to 15, which is not a decimal digit at all, and that is the difference a weighted code makes.

prompt: Match each BCD code to its representation of 9.2.
explanation: The digit 2 codes the same in all three, as 0010, because 2 is reachable by the same single weight in each. It is the 9 that separates them: 8 plus 1, then 4 plus 2 plus 2 plus 1, then 5 plus 4.

prompt: What is the 5421 BCD code for 9.2?
explanation: In 5421 the weights are 5, 4, 2, 1, so 9 is 5 plus 4, which is 1100. The 2 is 0010 as usual.

why.a: Correct. 1100 for the 9, 0010 for the 2.
why.b: Wrong. 1001 is the 8421 code for 9.
why.c: Wrong. 1111 is the 4221 code for 9.
why.d: Wrong on the second digit: 0100 would be 4 in 5421, not 2.

prompt: BCD code is described as useful for outputting to displays that are:

options.text: Always numeric, 0 to 9, such as digital clocks or digital voltmeters

explanation: Always numeric, and the deck names digital clocks and digital voltmeters. If a display can only show digits, coding digit by digit costs nothing and saves the conversion.

why.a: Correct, with both examples as given.
why.b: Wrong. Text needs an alphanumeric code such as ASCII.
why.c: Wrong. Graphics are covered separately, as bitmap and vector.
why.d: Wrong. Printers are mentioned as devices interfaced using alphanumeric codes.

prompt: The deck's two examples of always numeric displays are digital clocks and digital {{1}}.
explanation: Voltmeters. Both examples show only digits, which is the condition that makes BCD worthwhile.

prompt: Excess-3, also called XS3, is:

options.text: A non-weighted code used to express decimal numbers
A weighted code used to express decimal numbers
A method of representing negative numbers

explanation: Non-weighted. It has no per-bit weights at all, because the value is shifted by 3 before being coded.

why.a: Correct, and non-weighted is the word the exam has used.
why.b: Wrong, and this is the trap. BCD is weighted; Excess-3 is not.
why.c: Wrong. Character codes are ASCII, EBCDIC and Unicode.
why.d: Wrong. Excess-3 codes decimal digits, not signs.

prompt: Excess-3 is a weighted code, like 8421 BCD.
explanation: Excess-3 is explicitly non-weighted. In a weighted code you decode by adding the weights of the 1 bits; in Excess-3 you decode by subtracting 3.

why.true: Wrong. The deck introduces Excess-3 as a non-weighted code, in contrast to the three BCD codes.
why.false: Correct. It is non-weighted, which is exactly what separates it from BCD.

prompt: Excess-3 is significant for arithmetic because it overcomes a shortcoming of the 8421 BCD code when:

options.text: Adding two decimal digits whose sum exceeds 9
Adding two decimal digits whose sum is less than 9
Subtracting a larger digit from a smaller one

explanation: When two 8421 digits sum past 9 the result runs into the six unused bit patterns and has to be corrected. Excess-3 avoids that, which is why it is used in some old computers.

why.a: Correct, and the deck says exceeds 9 in exactly those words.
why.b: Wrong. Sums of 9 or less cause no trouble in 8421.
why.c: Wrong. Subtraction is not the case the slide names, though self-complementing does help there.
why.d: Wrong. Multiplication is not mentioned.

prompt: Excess-3 overcomes the shortcomings of the 8421 BCD code when adding two decimal digits whose sum exceeds {{1}}.
explanation: 9. Above 9 a single decimal digit will not hold the answer, and 8421 needs a correction step that Excess-3 does not.

prompt: How is the Excess-3 code for a decimal number formed?

options.text: Add 3 to each decimal digit, then replace each new digit by its four bit binary equivalent
Convert to binary, then add 3 to the result
Add 3 to the whole number, then convert to binary
Subtract 3 from each decimal digit, then convert

explanation: Add 3 per digit first, then code each digit in four bits. Doing it to the whole number instead of digit by digit is the usual mistake.

why.a: Correct, and the order matters: add first, then code.
why.b: Wrong. Adding after conversion would change the value, not the code.
why.c: Wrong. The 3 is added to each digit separately, not to the number as a whole.
why.d: Wrong. Subtracting 3 is how you decode Excess-3, not how you form it.

prompt: The Excess-3 code is determined by adding {{1}} to each decimal digit and then replacing each digit by its four bit binary equivalent.
explanation: 3, which is where the name comes from: the code is in excess of the true value by 3.

prompt: What is the XS3 code of 24?
explanation: 2 plus 3 is 5, which is 0101, and 4 plus 3 is 7, which is 0111. So 24 becomes 0101 0111.

why.a: Correct. 2 plus 3 is 5, which is 0101, and 4 plus 3 is 7, which is 0111.
why.b: Wrong. That is plain 8421 BCD for 24, with no 3 added.
why.c: Wrong. The digits are the right ones but in the wrong order.
why.d: Wrong. The second digit should be 7, which is 0111, not 4.

prompt: For the XS3 code of 24, the digit 2 becomes {{1}} and the digit 4 becomes {{2}} before being written in binary.
explanation: 5 and 7. Then 0101 and 0111.

prompt: Excess-3 is self-complementing, which means:

options.text: The 1's complement of an Excess-3 number is the Excess-3 code for the 9's complement of the corresponding decimal number
The 1's complement of an Excess-3 number is the Excess-3 code for the same decimal number
The 2's complement of an Excess-3 number is its own negative
The code needs no complement operation at all

explanation: Flip the bits and you get the 9's complement for free. That is what makes Excess-3 useful in some arithmetic operations.

why.a: Correct, and the deck's worked case is 6 giving 3.
why.b: Wrong. If it gave the same number back the property would be useless.
why.c: Wrong. The property is about the 1's complement, and about the 9's complement in decimal.
why.d: Wrong. The complement is exactly what is being taken.

prompt: The 1's complement of an Excess-3 number is the Excess-3 code for the {{1}}'s complement of the corresponding decimal number.
explanation: The 9's complement, since the digits run 0 to 9 and the 9's complement of a digit d is 9 minus d.

prompt: The Excess-3 code for decimal 6 is 1001. Taking its 1's complement gives 0110. Which decimal digit does 0110 stand for in Excess-3?
explanation: 0110 is 6, and subtracting the excess of 3 gives 3. And 3 is the 9's complement of 6, since 9 minus 6 is 3, which is exactly the property being demonstrated.

why.a: Correct. 6 minus 3 is 3, the 9's complement of the original 6.
why.b: Wrong. 6 is the number we started from; its code is 1001.
why.c: Wrong. 9 in Excess-3 would be 12, which is 1100.
why.d: Wrong. 0 in Excess-3 is 3, which is 0011.

prompt: The Excess-3 code for decimal 6 is {{1}}, and its 1's complement is {{2}}.
explanation: 6 plus 3 is 9, which is 1001. Flipping every bit gives 0110.

prompt: What is the Excess-3 code for 27?
explanation: 2 plus 3 is 5, which is 0101, and 7 plus 3 is 10, which is 1010. Together, 01011010.

why.a: Correct. 2 plus 3 is 5, which is 0101, and 7 plus 3 is 10, which is 1010.
why.b: Wrong. That is plain 8421 BCD for 27.
why.c: Wrong. That is the Excess-3 code for 24, from the earlier example.
why.d: Wrong. The two nibbles are the right ones but reversed.

prompt: The Excess-3 code for 597 is {{1}}.
explanation: 5 plus 3 is 8 which is 1000, 9 plus 3 is 12 which is 1100, 7 plus 3 is 10 which is 1010. So 100011001010, exactly as the deck prints it.

prompt: To convert an Excess-3 code back to decimal, after grouping into fours from the radix point you:

options.text: Take the 1's complement of each group
Shift each group right by three places

explanation: Subtract 0011, which is 3, from every group. Encoding adds 3, so decoding takes it back off.

why.a: Correct. Subtract 3 per group.
why.b: Wrong. Adding is the encoding direction.
why.c: Wrong. The 1's complement gives the 9's complement, which is a different property.
why.d: Wrong. Shifting divides by powers of 2 and has nothing to do with the excess.

prompt: To decode Excess-3, first make groups of {{1}} bits starting from the radix point.
explanation: Four bits per group, since each group codes one decimal digit. Starting from the radix point matters, because that is what makes a short leading group pad correctly.

prompt: The Excess-3 code 1000110 decodes to which decimal number?
explanation: Grouped from the radix point and padded, 1000110 becomes 0100 0110. Subtracting 0011 from each group gives 0001 0011, which is 13.

why.a: Correct. 13, as the deck's worked example gives it.
why.b: Wrong. That reads the groups as plain BCD without subtracting the excess.
why.c: Wrong. That reads the padded groups as BCD, again with no subtraction.
why.d: Wrong. Subtracting 3 once from the whole number rather than from each group gives this kind of error.

prompt: Subtracting 0011 from each group of the Excess-3 code 1000110 gives the new number {{1}}, whose decimal equivalent is {{2}}.
explanation: 00010011, which reads as BCD 1 then 3, so 13.

prompt: Earlier computers were used only for the purpose of calculations, that is, only as a calculating device.
explanation: The deck opens the alphanumeric codes section this way, to explain why letters and symbols needed encoding at all.

why.true: Correct. Only as a calculating device is the deck's phrase.
why.false: Wrong. This is the opening sentence of the alphanumeric codes section.

prompt: Why does a computer need alphanumeric codes to deal with letters and symbols?

options.text: Because it is a digital system and can only deal with 1's and 0's
Because letters take up more space than numbers
Because keyboards send letters in a different order
Because the ALU cannot perform logic operations on letters

explanation: The machine has only two symbols, so every letter and mark has to be given a binary pattern. That is what an alphanumeric code is.

why.a: Correct, and it is the same argument that gave base 2 in the first place.
why.b: Wrong. Space is not the reason given.
why.c: Wrong. Keyboard order is not discussed.
why.d: Wrong. Once a letter is a bit pattern the ALU can operate on it perfectly well.

prompt: A computer is a digital system and can only deal with {{1}} and 0's, so it uses alphanumeric codes for letters and symbols.
explanation: 1's and 0's. Two symbols only, so everything else has to be coded into them.

prompt: Alphanumeric codes are also called:
explanation: Character codes. They are binary codes used to represent alphanumeric data.

why.a: Correct, and the deck gives both names on the same line.
why.b: Wrong. Weighted describes BCD.
why.c: Wrong. Self-complementing describes Excess-3.
why.d: Wrong. BCD codes digits, not letters and punctuation.

prompt: Alphanumeric codes write which kinds of data in a form a computer can process?
explanation: Four kinds. Images are handled by the graphics section, as bitmap or vector, not by a character code.

why.a: Correct, letters of the alphabet head the list.
why.b: Correct, numbers are included, which is why a character code can print a digit.
why.c: Correct, mathematical symbols are third.
why.d: Correct, punctuation marks close the list.
